paper_summary: This paper presents GRADINO, a from-scratch generator and benchmark framework for numerical question answering over multiple non-relational (i.e., presentation-driven, pivoted, hierarchical, noisy) tables. GRADINO synthesizes a latent relational source (schema + dense table) using an LLM, derives executable SQL queries over that latent source to compute gold answers, and then renders answer-preserving perturbed non-relational views (pivoted layouts, merged headers, unit variations, OCR noise, blanks, footnotes). It supports two multi-table evidence-flow topologies: parallel (extract one scalar from each view then aggregate) and sequential (lookup chains where intermediate outputs become keys for subsequent views). The system verbalizes SQL into NL questions and verifies them; the authors release generation prompts, verification prompts, and generation statistics. Experiments across financial and environmental domains evaluate several LLMs (gpt-5-mini, Qwen variants) showing steep accuracy drops as table count increases and under unit heterogeneity; they validate findings on perturbed real tables, manually inspect generated questions (high correctness), and show GRADINO data can augment scarce in-domain supervision.
summary_of_strengths: 1) Clear problem framing: identifies an important and under-explored ‘non-relational multi-table’ blind spot for Table QA and LLMs. 2) Methodological contribution: a principled pipeline that decouples SQL supervision from non-relational presentation, enabling verifiable answers while systematically controlling perturbations, table count, and topology. 3) Practical benchmark and tooling: generation infrastructure, prompts, constraint mechanism (Z3-based sampling), and released data/code that enable reproducible, extensible evaluation. 4) Thorough empirical study: experiments across two domains, multiple models and scales, ablations for scaling, unit heterogeneity, parallel vs sequential patterns, and validation on perturbed real tables. 5) Useful findings: quantifies large, domain-dependent performance drops (especially with units and many tables) and shows GRADINO data can improve fine-tuned models when combined with scarce real supervision.
summary_of_weaknesses: 1) Synthetic realism: although the authors discuss this, GRADINO’s from-scratch tables may not fully capture visual/layout/semantic idiosyncrasies of many real spreadsheets and reports (alignment cues, charts, richer layout cues). This limits immediate external validity. 2) Scope restricted to numerical QA: the generator and evaluation focus on scalar numerical aggregation-style questions; non-numerical multi-table reasoning (set operations, textual joins, logical inference) is not studied. 3) Dependence on LLM generation and verification: many pipeline stages (schema proposal, constraint inference, NL verbalization and verification) are LLM-driven and could introduce biases or brittle failures; although the authors filter and inspect outputs, this dependence might affect portability and fairness. 4) Question verbalization reliability: sequential questions are more error-prone and NL fidelity is empirically validated but not guaranteed by construction; potential remaining hallucinations may influence measured model errors. 5) Model/evaluation breadth: experiments evaluate strong closed and open models but do not include a wider variety of recent LLM families or evaluation using automated program-execution baselines (e.g., tool-augmented execution), which might help pinpoint error causes.
comments_suggestions_typos: Suggestions to improve the paper and future work: (a) increase experiments on more naturally occurring multi-table documents (e.g., corporate reports, scraped spreadsheets) where feasible, or provide a small human-curated held-out set to better measure real-world transfer; (b) expand to non-numerical multi-table question types in future work or clarify how the pipeline generalizes; (c) provide more analysis of failure modes (retrieval of the correct cell vs conversion errors vs arithmetic mistakes) possibly via error categorization on a sampled subset; (d) make the semi-automatic constraint-editing UI and the discarded-generation statistics more prominent so users can assess generation efficiency; (e) minor: a few long paragraphs could be tightened for readability (e.g., merging similar limitations across sections). No critical typos detected that obstruct understanding.
limitations_and_societal_impact: The authors explicitly discuss key limitations (synthetic realism, restricted numerical focus, question-verbalization errors) and potential interpretive risks (that performance on synthetic benchmarks does not guarantee real-world reliability). They also explain data-privacy choices (all generated data is fictional) and use of public datasets for validation. Outstanding items for fuller discussion: potential domain or language biases introduced by LLM-driven schema and label generation (terminology choices may favor some linguistic forms), how varied unit-system conventions across locales/languages would be handled, and the risk that synthetic benchmarks could be misused to claim robustness beyond what real data shows. Overall the paper makes a conscientious effort to address limitations but could expand discussion on language/locale representation and on guidance for practitioners about appropriate use of synthetic evaluations.
ethical_concerns: No major ethical concerns detected. The authors generate fictional entities, avoid scraping private data, and report using public datasets only for validation. They acknowledge the interpretive risk of overgeneralizing synthetic benchmark performance. Nothing in the submission appears to violate ACL Code of Ethics; dual-use risk is low but users should not conflate synthetic benchmark success with production safety.
